15.title: the congregation
15.hook: the congregation; why Sikhs never practice alone for long
15.howItsDone: Sikhs gather as a sangat in the gurdwara to sing kirtan, listen to the scripture, pray Ardas and eat langar together; many also meet in homes for readings and hymn-singing.

screen: `DAY FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Last week ended with the three pillars: earn it clean, share it first, keep the name. Week three starts with the people around you. Day fifteen.
screen: `EARN IT CLEAN, SHARE IT FIRST, KEEP THE NAME.` → `WEEK THREE.`

segments.voice: Around certain people, a person gets funnier, kinder, braver. Around others, more anxious and quicker to gossip. Nobody gives an order; the room just does it. It's why parents want to meet their kids' friends. People become, a little at a time, like the people they sit with. The Gurus built that plain fact into the center of Sikh life.
screen: `FUNNIER AROUND SOME PEOPLE.` → `ANXIOUS AROUND OTHERS.` → `WE BECOME OUR COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Sangat. The congregation, the company you keep. You'll often hear sadh sangat, the company of the holy. Everywhere Guru Nanak traveled, the stories say, he left a sangat behind: a small circle of people who met to sing the hymns, share food and look after one another. Long before there were grand buildings, there were these circles of ordinary people. So what makes a sangat true? The scripture asks that very question, and the answer, in paraphrase, is simple: where the one name is spoken. Not where the building is finest or the people richest. Sikhs speak of the sangat with a startling kind of respect. There's a long tradition that the Guru is present wherever the sangat gathers, and that the congregation, deciding together, carries real weight. That's why so much of Sikh life happens with others. Not because time alone is bad; remembering on your own breath matters. But a person alone tends to drift, and a person in good company gets carried, the way a small boat is carried by a current.
screen: `SANGAT — THE COMPANY YOU KEEP.` · `NANAK LEFT A CIRCLE BEHIND.` · `WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · `A PERSON ALONE DRIFTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you spend the most time with. Not to judge them; just notice. Who do you leave feeling lighter? Who helps you remember what matters? Picture one of them clearly, and let yourself be grateful for them, and stay there a while.
Sangat. The congregation, the company you keep, gathered around the one name. Fifteenth word.
screen: `SANGAT — your 15th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: good company. You can't choose every room you're in, but you can choose some of them. Day fifteen.

screen: `DAY 15 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DOOR OF THE GURU.`

16.title: the door of the guru
16.hook: the door of the guru; why it's open to anyone
16.carry: cover your head, take off your shoes, come in
16.howItsDone: Anyone may visit a gurdwara: visitors cover their heads, remove their shoes and wash their hands, sit on the floor before the Guru Granth Sahib for kirtan, receive karah prashad, and eat in the langar.

screen: `DAY SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: sangat. Your line was good company. Today, the place where that company meets. Day sixteen.
screen: `SANGAT — GOOD COMPANY.` → `DAY 16.`

segments.voice: On a street you know, there's a tall flag, saffron or blue, on a pole outside a building: maybe a white one with domes, maybe a converted warehouse or an old church. Through the door you can hear singing and drums, and smell something cooking. And someone walking by might wonder: can I just walk in? Today, the answer.
screen: `A TALL FLAG ON A POLE.` → `SINGING, DRUMS, SOMETHING COOKING.` → `CAN I JUST WALK IN?`

segments.voice: Gurdwara. Gur, the Guru. Dwara, a door. The door of the Guru. The flag from day seven, the Nishan Sahib, is there so it can be found from far away. And yes: anyone can walk in, of any faith or none. In Amritsar, the Golden Temple was built with doors on all four sides, which Sikhs explain as a welcome from every direction. There are a few things everyone does, Sikh or not. Cover your head; gurdwaras usually keep scarves at the door. Take off your shoes. Wash your hands. Leave tobacco and alcohol outside. That's all. Inside, the last two weeks meet under one roof. At the front, on a raised platform under a canopy, rests the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib. People bow, then sit on the floor, all at one level: the sangat. Musicians sing the hymns: naam japna, out loud. Near the end comes the Ardas, then karah prashad, a warm sweet of flour, butter and sugar, placed in cupped hands. Then the langar. And the people cooking, cleaning and minding the shoes? That's seva. A gurdwara is the whole path, given a building and a door that stays open.
screen: `GUR, THE GURU. DWARA, A DOOR.` · `OPEN TO ANYONE, FROM EVERY SIDE.` · `HEAD COVERED, SHOES OFF, HANDS WASHED.` · `THE WHOLE PATH UNDER ONE ROOF.`

segments.voice: Do the threshold with your body. Lift your hands to your head, as if laying a cloth over it. Rub your palms together slowly, as if rinsing them. Feel your feet on the floor, bare or as if they were. Then stay at the door a while, listening: singing somewhere inside, and nobody asking who you are.
The gurdwara. The door of the Guru: the Sikh place of worship, open to anyone. Sixteenth word.
screen: `THE GURDWARA — your 16th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: cover your head, take off your shoes, come in. That's all a first visit asks of anyone. Day sixteen.

screen: `DAY 16 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVER-RISING SPIRITS.`

17.title: ever-rising spirits
17.hook: ever-rising spirits — optimism as a discipline
17.tomorrow: what a sikh carries and why
17.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of chardi kala in everyday greetings and answers, and ask for it at the close of the Ardas prayer; it is taught as a lasting optimism rooted in trust in God's will.

screen: `DAY SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the gurdwara. Your line was cover your head, take off your shoes, come in. Today, a two-word answer to how are you. Day seventeen.
screen: `THE GURDWARA — COME IN.` → `DAY 17.`

segments.voice: Ask a Sikh grandfather how he's doing. He's eighty-one, his knees are bad, and the doctor's news this week wasn't great. There's a decent chance he'll smile and say two words: chardi kala. Not I'm fine. Something more like: spirits rising. He's noticed everything. He's just decided which way his spirit is going to face.
screen: `BAD KNEES, HARD NEWS.` → `CHARDI KALA.` → `NOT A MOOD. A DISCIPLINE.`

segments.voice: Chardi kala. Chardi means rising, climbing. Kala means spirit, energy, a state of being. Ever-rising spirits. Here's the difference between chardi kala and just being cheerful. Cheerfulness depends on circumstances. Chardi kala is meant to hold when circumstances collapse. And Sikh history has asked a great deal of it. There were long stretches, especially in the eighteenth century, when Sikhs were hunted, driven into forests and hills. Out of those years came a whole defiant way of speaking: tradition remembers that a lone Sikh might call himself sava lakh, a hundred and twenty-five thousand. One man, a whole army. Not denial: a refusal to let circumstances write your spirit for you. Where does it come from? From trust. Sikhs speak of hukam, the will of God running through everything. If all of life, even the hard parts, is held inside the one, despair doesn't get the last word. You heard the phrase on day five: the Ardas asks for it near its very end. And chardi kala doesn't forbid sadness. Sikhs grieve, and weep. It just keeps pointing up, like a plant that grows toward the light in a dark room.
screen: `CHARDI — RISING. KALA — SPIRIT.` · `NOT CHEERFULNESS. IT HOLDS WHEN THINGS FALL.` · `ONE SIKH, A WHOLE ARMY.` · `TRUST IN HUKAM, THE WILL OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Let one heavy thing come to mind, something that's actually hard right now. Don't push it away. Then, without denying any of it, let your posture rise a little: lift your chest, soften your face, breathe in as if drawing yourself upward. You're not saying it's fine. You're choosing which way your spirit faces. Stay there, with the weight and the rising together.
Chardi kala. Ever-rising spirits: hope practiced as a discipline, holding even when life is hard. Seventeenth word.
screen: `CHARDI KALA — your 17th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: rise anyway. Not pretending it's fine; just choosing which way to face. Day seventeen.

screen: `DAY 17 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT A SIKH CARRIES AND WHY.`

18.title: what a sikh carries and why
18.hook: what a Sikh carries and why
18.tomorrow: the tenth guru, the khalsa, the saint-soldier
18.howItsDone: Sikhs initiated into the Khalsa keep the five Ks at all times: uncut hair, a wooden comb, a steel bracelet, a cotton undergarment and a small sword. Many other Sikhs wear the kara.

screen: `DAY EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: chardi kala. Your line was rise anyway. Today, five things some Sikhs carry every day. Day eighteen.
screen: `CHARDI KALA — RISE ANYWAY.` → `DAY 18.`

segments.voice: A wedding ring turned during a hard meeting. A photo in a wallet. A grandmother's watch that doesn't keep time anymore. Small things people carry to remember. They don't do anything, exactly. Touch one, and something comes back: a promise, a person, who someone meant to be. Initiated Sikhs carry five of them, every day.
screen: `A RING, A PHOTO, A WATCH.` → `TOUCH IT, AND SOMETHING COMES BACK.` → `A SIKH CARRIES FIVE.`

segments.voice: They're the five Ks, because in Punjabi each one begins with the sound k. Sikhs initiated into the Khalsa, the family that began with the five on day four, keep all five. Kesh: uncut hair, from day three, under the turban. Kanga: a small wooden comb tucked into the hair. Keep the hair clean and ordered, and the life too. Kara: the steel circle on the wrist, also from day three. Kachera: a cotton undergarment, like simple shorts: self-restraint, and readiness to move. Kirpan: a small sword, worn in a sheath, often under the clothes. It stands for the duty to protect people who can't protect themselves, and for dignity and courage. It isn't there for aggression. Notice what all five have in common. None is a decoration. A comb, a bracelet, underwear, hair: plain, ordinary things. The reminders aren't locked away in a temple. They're on the body, at work, at the gym, all day. Faith you can touch. Many Sikhs who aren't initiated still wear the kara, and wherever you are with the rest, this path starts from there.
screen: `FIVE THINGS THAT BEGIN WITH K.` · `KESH AND KANGA — HAIR, AND ITS COMB.` · `KARA — THE HAND REMEMBERS.` · `KACHERA AND KIRPAN — RESTRAINT, PROTECTION.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing you're wearing or carrying: a ring, a watch, a hair tie, your sleeve. Put your hand on it and decide, just for now, what it will remind you of: something you believe, a person, a promise. Close your hand around it and breathe with that meaning for a while.
The five Ks. Kesh, kanga, kara, kachera, kirpan: five reminders a committed Sikh carries every day. Eighteenth word.
screen: `THE FIVE KS — your 18th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: reminders you can touch. Faith that goes where you go, not left behind at the door. Day eighteen.

screen: `DAY 18 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TENTH GURU, THE KHALSA, THE SAINT-SOLDIER.`

19.title: the tenth guru, the khalsa, the saint-soldier
19.hook: the tenth Guru, the Khalsa, the saint-soldier
19.tomorrow: a scripture that is the guru
19.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Gobind Singh as the tenth Guru and founder of the Khalsa, celebrate his birth each year, recite his compositions in daily prayers, and speak of the ideal of the sant sipahi, the saint-soldier.

screen: `DAY NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five Ks. Your line was reminders you can touch. Today, the Guru they trace back to. Day nineteen.
screen: `THE FIVE KS — REMINDERS YOU CAN TOUCH.` → `DAY 19.`

segments.voice: Nine years old. A father leaving home, knowing he may not come back. He has gone to the capital to stand up for the right of people from another faith to practice theirs, and he doesn't come back. Now the community turns to the boy and tells him: you are the Guru. That's how the tenth Guru's leadership began, in 1675, as Sikh tradition tells it. The boy grew into a poet, a warrior and the founder of the Khalsa.
screen: `NINE YEARS OLD.` → `A FATHER WHO DOESN'T COME BACK.` → `YOU ARE THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth and last human Guru of the Sikhs. His father was the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur. Sikh tradition remembers that he went to Delhi on behalf of Hindu Kashmiri pandits who were being pressed to convert, and was executed there by the Mughal authorities. Sikhs honor him as a martyr who gave his life for the freedom of others to worship. That memory shaped his son. Guru Gobind Singh taught that a person of faith should be two things at once. The Sikh phrase is sant sipahi: saint and soldier. Saint, because the inner life comes first: remembrance, humility, the name. Soldier, because when the weak are being crushed, a saint doesn't look away. The kirpan from yesterday comes from exactly this. And the order matters. A soldier with no saint in him is only violence; a saint with no courage may stand by while others suffer. He wrote devotional poetry Sikhs still recite every day, and in 1699 he called the five from day four out of the crowd. He lost his father, and all four of his sons, to the violence of his time, and is still remembered for chardi kala. And near the end of his life he decided there would be no eleventh human Guru.
screen: `THE TENTH AND LAST HUMAN GURU.` · `A FATHER WHO DIED FOR OTHERS' FREEDOM.` · `SANT SIPAHI — SAINT AND SOLDIER.` · `THE SAINT COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Let one hand rest open on your lap: that's the saint, quiet, open, remembering. Let the other close into a gentle fist: that's the courage to stand up for someone. Feel both at once. Now think of one person in your life who might need someone to stand up for them, and hold them in mind, with both hands.
Guru Gobind Singh. The tenth Guru, founder of the Khalsa, poet and warrior: the saint-soldier. Nineteenth word.
screen: `GURU GOBIND SINGH — your 19th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: sword and saint. The saint comes first, and the courage serves it. Day nineteen.

screen: `DAY 19 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A SCRIPTURE THAT IS THE GURU.`

20.title: a scripture that is the guru
20.hook: a scripture that is the Guru; why it's carried, covered, put to bed
20.howItsDone: In every gurdwara the Guru Granth Sahib rests under a canopy on a raised platform, is attended with a chaur, opened at dawn and put to rest at night; a hymn read each morning is taken as the day's hukamnama.

screen: `DAY TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guru Gobind Singh. Your line was sword and saint. Today, who he named to come after him. Day twenty.
screen: `GURU GOBIND SINGH — SWORD AND SAINT.` → `DAY 20.`

segments.voice: Late evening at a gurdwara. The last hymn has been sung. Someone gently closes a very large book, wraps it in embroidered cloth, and lifts it onto their head. Someone else waves a whisk of long white hair over it, the way attendants once did for a king. It's carried to its own room, laid on a bed and covered for the night. At dawn it's carried back out and opened, and the day begins. Why would anyone put a book to bed?
screen: `A LARGE BOOK, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `CARRIED ON SOMEONE'S HEAD.` → `PUT TO BED FOR THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Guru Granth Sahib. Granth means book. Sahib is a word of deep respect. And Guru, the teacher from day one. The Guru who is a book. Here's how that happened. The fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him and his own, and in 1604 installed the collection at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. Then, in 1708, near the end of his life, Guru Gobind Singh declared there would be no more human Gurus. From then on, Sikhs would find their Guru in the scripture. So when Sikhs bow before it, they aren't bowing to paper and ink. They're bowing to the Guru, present in the words. That's why it's treated like a revered teacher in the room: higher than everyone, under a canopy, attended with a whisk, put to rest at night. And inside? Hymns by six of the Gurus, and, remarkably, by holy poets who weren't Sikhs at all: Kabir, a weaver; Ravidas, from a caste many looked down on; Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi. Almost all of it is poetry, arranged by musical mode, meant to be sung. Every morning, gurdwaras open it and read the first hymn on the page as the hukamnama, the order of the day. Sikhs don't only read this book. They listen to it.
screen: `GRANTH — BOOK. SAHIB — RESPECT.` · `1708: NO MORE HUMAN GURUS.` · `TREATED LIKE A TEACHER IN THE ROOM.` · `GURUS AND SAINTS, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Think of words that have spoken to you: a line from a book, a letter, something someone once said that you've never forgotten. Bring it to mind as exactly as you can. Now imagine those words not as print, but as someone sitting beside you, saying them to you now. Let them speak, and just listen.
The Guru Granth Sahib. The Sikh scripture, honored as the living Guru since 1708, holding the Gurus' hymns and the words of other saints. Twentieth word.
screen: `THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB — your 20th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a living book. Read as if someone were speaking to you today. Day twenty.

screen: `DAY 20 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOUNTAIN AHEAD.`

21.title: the mountain ahead
21.hook: the mountain ahead; Nanak's morning prayer
21.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the daily prayers (Nitnem) recite Japji Sahib each morning, often before dawn after bathing, as the first of them; children often learn it by heart a stanza at a time.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Guru Granth Sahib. Your line was a living book. Today, the poem it opens with, and the last day of camp one.
screen: `THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB — A LIVING BOOK.` → `DAY 21.`

segments.voice: It's still dark outside. Four in the morning, maybe five. In homes in Punjab, London, Toronto, California and Nairobi, someone is already up. They've bathed. They sit quietly, cover their head, and begin to recite a long poem, often from memory. Some learned it as children, a verse at a time, beside a grandparent before school. It's the first thing in the scripture and the first thing in their day.
screen: `FOUR IN THE MORNING.` → `A LONG POEM, FROM MEMORY.` → `THE FIRST THING IN THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Japji Sahib. Jap, to recite, the same root as naam japna. Ji and Sahib, words of love and respect. It's Guru Nanak's great poem, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib. It begins with the root verse from days ten and eleven. Then a short verse that the translator Macauliffe gave like this: "The True One was in the beginning; the True One was in the primal age." Then come thirty-eight stanzas, called pauris, steps or rungs, like a ladder, and a closing verse that pictures air as the Guru, water as the father, and the earth as the great mother of all. Inside, it's full of questions. Can you think your way to God? Not if you think a hundred thousand times, the first stanza says. What will do it? Living within hukam, God's will, the word from day seventeen. It's the first of the daily prayers, and nobody has to start with all of it: many begin with the root verse, then a stanza, then a little more. That's why your line is a promise. Later on this path, we'll climb Japji verse by verse. And look how far you've come. Waheguru, langar, the turban, the Panj Pyare, Ardas, Sikh, the Khanda.
